question: Who can work on a plain English project according to the handbook?
answer: A plain English project can be handled by a team or by one person working alone.
evidence: Many of you routinely select a team to think and talk about how to write a document from scratch or rewrite an existing document. Or you may do it on your own. In that case, rest assured that one person can do it alone.

question: Why should writers consider how investors will read a document?
answer: Writers should consider whether investors will read the document straight through or skip around to sections that interest them.
evidence: How will they read the document for the first time? Will they read it straight through or skip around to the sections that interest them?

question: What is the first principle of good document organization?
answer: The first principle is to present the big picture before the details.
evidence: First, present the big picture before the details.
evidence_points: First, present the big picture before the details.

question: What are the common problems found in disclosure documents?
answer: Common problems include long sentences, passive voice, weak verbs, superfluous words, legal and financial jargon, numerous defined terms, abstract words, unnecessary details, and unreadable design and layout.
evidence: Common problems • Long sentences • Passive voice • Weak verbs • Superfluous words • Legal and financial jargon • Numerous defined terms • Abstract words • Unnecessary details • Unreadable design and layout

question: Why should writers replace abstract terms with concrete terms?
answer: Concrete terms help readers form clearer mental images and therefore make concepts and situations easier to understand.
evidence: And yet, it’s far easier to comprehend a concept or a situation when your mind can form images. You can make complex information more understandable by giving your readers an example using one investor.

question: Why should writers avoid creating new acronyms?
answer: New acronyms force readers to memorize a new vocabulary while they are already trying to understand complicated concepts.
evidence: Don’t create new jargon that’s unique to your document in the form of acronyms or other words. It’s asking too much of your readers to memorize a new vocabulary while they are trying to understand complicated concepts.
